To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
carbohydrate intake during the recovery from exercise does not affect the inflammation response (IL-6 and CRP) or muscle damage response (CK and strength).
carbohydrate supplementation during the 2-d postexercise recovery did not influence the delayed inflammatory response, as measured by plasma interleukin- (IL) 6.
carbohydrate supplementation during the initial recovery period from eccentric exercise does not influence inflammation or muscle damage markers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of carbohydrate ingestion on muscle damage markers and inflammatory cytokines.
the effect of carbohydrate ingestion on inflammation and muscle-damage response following eccentric exercise.
the effects of carbohydrate supplementation on the inflammatory response following exercise-induced muscle damage and the subsequent recovery process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

carbohydrate supplementation during the recovery from exercise does not appear to have any effect on the delayed IL- 6 response, which is temporally linked to the inflammatory response, and does not influence muscle damage or soreness.
carbohydrate ingestion during recovery does not influence the inflammatory and muscle-damage response.
the carbohydrate supplementation does not influence the inflammatory response and muscle damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

carbohydrate supplementation during the early recovery period after eccentric exercise does not influence inflammation (IL- 6, CRP), muscle damage (muscle soreness, strength loss, and CK activity) or blood glucose.

carbohydrate supplementation during the recovery phase from eccentric exercise does not influence delayed IL-6 responses temporally linked to muscle inflammation and does not affect muscle-damage responses.
carbohydrate supplementation does not affect the inflammatory and muscle-damage response following exercise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the timing of the carbohydrate intake is not important for the recovery from the muscle-damaging exercise.
carbohydrate intake is not detrimental to the inflammatory and muscle-damage response following a bout of eccentric exercise.
carbohydrate supplementation does not seem to affect the immune and muscle-damage response to exercise-induced muscle soreness.
